scores.evidence: Channels listed (F1) cover website, Facebook-Instagram, email list, and paid ads — a reasonable spread on paper. In practice (B4) tells the real story: "Instagram, honestly. Reels of Bramble (my noise-phobic collie cross) doing settle training in her coat drive most first orders" — one organic channel is doing almost all acquisition heavy lifting. Paid experiments have not held: (F3) reports "Google Shopping ads — £600 over two months, because in a thumbnail our £58 coat looks identical to the £14 one" and a craft fair in Cirencester described as "wrong crowd entirely, sold two feeders." A video channel is listed in A3 but never cited as a traffic source. The business is visible to people who already follow Bramble; it is largely invisible to rescue owners who don't.
scores.leak_cost_estimate: £300/mo confirmed wasted (= £600 Google Shopping over 2 months per F3). At £52 per sale, that is approximately 6 sales per month unearned from paid search — a channel that received real budget and returned no noted conversions.

scores.evidence: The A2 pitch is specific and honest: "We make calming kit for anxious dogs — a pressure coat, a den bed, slow feeders — all of it road-tested on a panel of genuinely nervous rescues before we'll sell a single one." That is a clear, differentiated statement. On Instagram, where there is room to show Bramble and tell the rescue-trial story, it converts — B4 confirms Reels drive most first orders. But (F3) reveals where the message breaks down: "in a thumbnail our £58 coat looks identical to the £14 one." The premium story is channel-dependent; strip away the context and it disappears entirely.
scores.leak_cost_estimate: £600 in Google Shopping spend (F3) returned no noted conversions against a £52 average sale — that is approximately 11 sales that paid search was paid to deliver and did not. These were customers actively searching; the message failed to earn them.

scores.evidence: Two functioning routes exist. The organic Instagram path works (B4). The email series is the strongest conversion asset in the business — (F4): "the five-part introduction-guide email series — people who read all five emails buy the bundle at nearly triple the rate." But both routes depend on the customer arriving through a warm channel. There is no described landing page, product page structure, or CTA for paid or cold traffic. The best conversion tool sits behind an opt-in that a new visitor arriving from Google Shopping would likely never reach. The (F3) spend produced no notable return, which is consistent with a conversion path that was never built for cold arrivals.
scores.leak_cost_estimate: £260/mo (= 5 new customers/month who encounter the site without the email series context and buy a single item rather than a bundle × £52 additional sale value per bundle uplift — a deliberately conservative count of 5).

scores.evidence: The five-part welcome series is a genuine asset and (F4) proves it. But (F2) is the concern: "About 2,400 subscribers. Last proper send was mid-June — a Bramble update plus the Den Bed restock. I aim for fortnightly and manage monthly, which needs fixing before October." That gap — mid-June to at least late summer — means a warm, opted-in list has been silent through the run-up to fireworks season, the single highest-anxiety period in the anxious-dog calendar. No post-purchase sequence, abandoned-cart flow, or win-back campaign is mentioned. The infrastructure beyond the welcome series appears thin.
scores.leak_cost_estimate: £1,248/mo per missed fortnightly send (= 2,400 subscribers × 1% conservative single-send conversion rate × £52 average sale = 24 orders). One send missed per month at that rate is 24 unearned orders; over a six-week silence the cumulative cost is higher.

scores.evidence: The proof story is specific and rare — (E3): "Every product goes through a trial panel of twelve genuinely anxious rescue dogs before launch, and we publish the fail rate — the feeder took three redesigns and we say so." Publishing failure builds more trust than publishing success, and almost no brand does it. Bramble herself is living proof on Instagram. (F4) confirms word of mouth runs through rescue owner Facebook groups. The weakness is placement: this proof appears to live in Instagram content and the email series, not visibly on product pages or at the point a cold visitor is deciding whether to spend £58. No on-site review volume, star rating count, or trust badge is mentioned.
scores.leak_cost_estimate: £520/mo (= 10 cold first-time visitors per month who might have purchased with visible on-site proof but leave without it × £52 average sale — using a count of 10 as a minimum credible estimate).

scores.evidence: Premium positioning (E4) is backed by a real differentiator, and a 60%+ repeat rate (B6) confirms the product earns it. The bundle is the strongest commercial unit: (F4) confirms "people who read all five emails buy the bundle at nearly triple the rate." But the bundle is currently a reward for completing the full email series rather than a front-line offer. (E2) describes a specific competitive loss: "We also lose bundle sales to PawsRelax's £39 'starter set' when people shop on price alone" — a framed, proof-backed bundle visible on the site before any email opt-in could reframe that comparison before it becomes a price decision.
scores.leak_cost_estimate: £1,040/mo (= 20 of the 150 new monthly customers who never see the bundle on the website × £52 additional average sale value if they added one more item at point of first purchase — 20 customers × £52).

top_3_leaks: Dormant email list: 2,400 opted-in subscribers — people who already know Bramble — are being reached monthly at best, with (F2) admitting 'Last proper send was mid-June.' At a conservative 1% conversion per send and £52 per sale, one missed fortnightly email is ~£1,248 in unearned revenue. October and November are the highest-anxiety months in the anxious-dog calendar; every week of list silence between now and Bonfire Night is disproportionately costly.

Bundle offer hidden behind the full email series: (F4) proves triple bundle conversion for subscribers who read all five emails, but that gate means every customer who finds the website through search, paid ads, or a shared Reel link never sees the best offer the business has. The strongest commercial unit is invisible at the primary purchase entry point.

Paid search spend structurally misaligned with the product story: (F3) describes £600 over two months on Google Shopping where 'in a thumbnail our £58 coat looks identical to the £14 one' — the rescue-trial panel, the three-redesign feeder story, the handwritten guide, none of it fits a thumbnail. Budget spent in a channel that strips away every differentiator Steady Hound has is not a targeting problem; it is a channel mismatch that will not improve with more spend.
quick_wins: Write and schedule three fortnightly emails this week — one for late October (Bramble's own bonfire night story and why the coat exists), one for early November ('is your rescue ready for fireworks?' linking directly to the coat product page), and one for mid-November (bundle gift reminder). Fireworks season is the single biggest natural purchase trigger for anxious-dog owners; the list has months of silence to recover from before it can convert.

Add a 'Start with the Bundle' section to the website homepage before the weekend — pull the rescue trial panel story and the three-redesign feeder detail verbatim from the email series copy and place it above the bundle SKU with a direct buy button. The proof that drives triple conversion in email should not require an opt-in to see.

Add a single CTA to the caption of every current pinned or active Instagram Reel this week — something like 'DM me BRAMBLE for the 5-part settling guide' or 'link in bio for the full rescue guide' — and make the email series sign-up the sole destination of the bio link. Since (F4) confirms email-series readers buy the bundle at nearly triple the rate, routing Reel viewers directly into the series is the highest-value action Steady Hound currently has available and it is not yet visible.
narrative_summary:
Steady Hound has something most small e-commerce brands would trade a great deal for: a product story that is genuinely true, a mascot in Bramble who turns scrollers into first-time buyers, and a repeat rate above 60% that proves the kit actually works for nervous dogs. The Instagram-to-first-order pipeline is real and functioning. The five-part email series is outstanding — triple bundle conversion is not a small number, and it tells you something important about your customers: trust sells this product. Price never will.

The gap between where you are and where you could be sits in three places. First, the email list. 2,400 people who already believe in the Bramble story are being reached monthly at best, and the last proper send was mid-June. That is a quiet, consistent leak — and it is going to cost more in October and November than any other two months of the year, because anxious-dog owners are at their most anxious and most ready to spend. Second, the bundle offer that converts so well in the email series is invisible to anyone who visits the site without going through all five emails. Your strongest commercial unit is hidden. Third, the £600 on Google Shopping taught you something worth keeping: a thumbnail cannot carry this story, and no amount of budget will fix that. Redirect it.

None of this is a product problem or an audience problem. Rescue dog owners are loyal, vocal, and community-minded — and you are already speaking their language. Bramble is doing the work. What needs fixing is consistency and sequencing: getting the proof that already exists in front of people earlier, and making sure a warm, well-built list hears from you before fireworks season is over.
